newsitem.title: ZAIRE: 1,200 refugees taken to Zaire airlift by train.
newsitem.headline: 1,200 refugees taken to Zaire airlift by train.

text.p: Some 1,200 Rwandan Hutu refugees arrived safely in the Zairean city of Kisangani on Tuesday in the first such trip since 92 were killed in a stampede two days ago.

"We had full control of the train and the whole operation went very smoothly," said Kilian Kleinschmidt, head of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR in Kisangani, after the train arrived without problems from Biaro camp 41 km (25 miles) to the south.
It was the first train from Biaro which had UNHCR staff on board and 20 Zairean Red Cross workers marshalled the refugees into wagons in groups of 20 at a time to prevent a stampede.
UNHCR complained however it still needed more cooperation from rebel authorities as the train was delayed for hours waiting for a rebel escort before being told one was not needed.
Aid workers also said rebel authorities were still dumping refugees by truck at a ferry point on a bank of the Zaire river without informing aid agencies of their arrival.
"They are packing them in like sardines," said one U.N. aid worker after a sea container full of refugees was left at the ferry. A man died in the container, aid workers said.
UNHCR said it evacuated 1,976 refugees on nine flights from Kisangani to Rwanda on Tuesday, bringing the total to be repatriated since the start of the airlift on April 27 to nearly 10,000.
"But we can only reach some 40,000 Rwandan refugees south of Kisangani," said UNHCR spokesman Peter Kessler. "There are still a lot of areas we are not being given access to and we need more
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.

UNHCR on Monday blamed a breakdown in coordination with rebel authorities for the death of the 92 Rwandan Hutu refugees crushed or suffocated on the train on Sunday. Another 45 injured refugees remain in hospital.
A UNHCR report said Hutu refugees swarmed on board the six open cars of the rebel-run train to Biaro camp at two stops, where as many as 5,000 to 6,000 people were waiting to board.
Survivors said thousands of refugees swarmed onto the train as it pulled out of a station near Biaro camp. Children, the weak and ill adults were forced to the bottom of the metal cars.
Rwanda's government on Tuesday demanded an international inquiry into the train disaster and blamed it on "gross inefficiency and mismanagement" by UNHCR.

Ephraim Kabaija, the head of Rwanda's joint commission for repatriation, said in a statement the refugees panicked because they had heard UNHCR intended to suspend the trains because its transit camp near Kisangani airport was full.

"The government is strongly concerned by this act of negligence and further urges the United Nations to stop the acts that prolong the suffering of the Rwandese," said Kabaija, adding Rwanda objected to anything slowing the refugee return.

Up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees south of Kisangani fled into the jungle two weeks ago after attacks by what they said were local Zaireans and rebels. Thousands have emerged in the last week, desperate to join the airlift to their homeland.
After weeks of delaying a U.N. airlift via Kisangani, citing a cholera outbreak, rebels said on April 27 U.N. agencies had 60 days from May 1 to repatriate all Rwandan refugees in Zaire.
